basics.name: PartNet-Mobility dataset / SAPIEN (SimulAted Part-based Interactive ENvironment), UC San Diego, Stanford University and Simon Fraser University
basics.url: https://huggingface.co/datasets/sapien-sim/PartNetMobility (now the main way to get the dataset, per the SAPIEN README); simulator code at https://github.com/haosulab/sapien (read through its raw readme.md); documentation at https://sapien-sim.github.io/docs/. The original browse site https://sapien.ucsd.edu/browse could not be opened from here (blocked) [uncertain: whether it is still live]
basics.resource_type: GitHub repo or dataset (a research dataset of 3D articulated everyday objects with labelled moving joints, plus an open-source physics simulator that loads them)
basics.cost: Free (dataset access requires an approved request; the simulator is free to install with pip)
basics.license: Dataset: custom research licence ('Terms of Use') from UCSD, Stanford and SFU: non-commercial research and educational use only, no warranty, the user indemnifies the universities, access can be terminated, and users must also follow the ShapeNet terms of use because the models build on ShapeNet (originally from 3D Warehouse). Hugging Face tags it 'license: other'. Simulator code: Apache License 2.0 (copyright UCSD SU Lab 2020-2024 and Hillbot Inc. 2025). For the encyclopedia: link to it, but do not copy its models or renders onto a public site
basics.year: SAPIEN paper and PartNet-Mobility dataset first released March 2020 (arXiv 2003.08515, 19 March 2020; CVPR 2020). The simulator reached version 3.0 with PhysX 5 GPU simulation [uncertain: exact release date]. The Hugging Face dataset repository was created 18 July 2026 and last updated 30 July 2026
basics.access_barrier: free login plus manual approval. On Hugging Face you must log in, give your full name, affiliation and purpose, and be verified through your account's primary email; university addresses are usually approved automatically, while generic addresses (Gmail, Outlook) may be rejected. Using the data then needs 3D and simulation software (Python, a GPU for the simulator)
basics.image_license: Same as the dataset: the textured models and any renders come from ShapeNet/3D Warehouse models and fall under the non-commercial research terms. The paper's figures are under the paper's copyright; no open image licence is stated [uncertain]
basics.authority_level: academic peer-reviewed (CVPR 2020), from the Hao Su lab at UC San Diego with Stanford (Leonidas Guibas) and Simon Fraser University (Angel X. Chang). Joint annotations were made by trained annotators with a purpose-built web tool

coverage.covers: 2,346 3D models of everyday indoor objects in 46 categories, with 14,068 movable parts, each connected by a labelled joint. Only 3 motion types are annotated: hinge (turning around an axis, e.g. doors, lids, laptop screens), slider (moving along an axis, e.g. drawers, buttons) and screw (turning and sliding on the same axis, e.g. bottle caps, swivel chair height), plus fixed parts and whole objects marked as 'fixed base' or 'free'. Hinges and sliders have motion limits (angles, lengths); screws record limits and whether the turn and slide are coupled. Categories include bottle, box, bucket, cabinet (storage furniture), camera, cart, chair, folding chair, clock, coffee machine, dishwasher, dispenser, door, eyeglasses, fan, faucet, fridge, globe, kettle, keyboard, knife, lamp, laptop, lighter, microwave, monitor, mouse, oven, pen, phone, pliers, pot, printer, remote, safe, scissors, stapler, suitcase, switch, table, toaster, toilet, trash can, USB stick, washing machine and window
coverage.organisation: By object category (46 everyday categories, e.g. faucet, laptop, stapler), with each object as a numbered folder (e.g. 100013) holding its URDF model, meshes and annotation files. The original SAPIEN website had a browse page with category filters and a 3D preview [uncertain: could not be opened]. On Hugging Face it is a flat list of 2,347 zip files named by object ID, with no browsing. Organising by everyday object is easy for beginners to understand, but it tells you where a joint appears, not what kind of connection it is
coverage.scope_match: low. It labels only three generic joint motions (hinge, slider, screw) on household objects, not connection or mechanism types. It has no latches, snap fits, ratchets, detents, torque limiters, gears, powered connectors or adhesives. It is mainly useful as a large set of real-world examples of where hinges, slides and screw caps are used, and for 'how does it move' vocabulary
coverage.taxonomy_used: Two layers. (1) Motion (joint) type, 3 annotated types: hinge (rotational, revolute), slider (translational, prismatic) and screw (combined hinge and slider), plus fixed joints and object-level labels 'fixed base', 'free' and 'outlier'. In the simulator, joints follow PhysX: revolute (hinge), prismatic (slider) and fixed; files are in URDF (Unified Robot Description Format), and the sources read do not say how screw joints are stored in it [uncertain]. (2) Object category, 46 top-level groups, with a category-specific semantic label for each moving part (e.g. door, drawer, lid, button) [uncertain: full label list not seen]
coverage.example_types: hinge joint (revolute joint) - door, lid, oven door, laptop screen, toilet seat; slider joint (prismatic joint) - drawer, keyboard key, push button, sliding window; screw joint (helical motion, turning plus sliding) - bottle cap, swivel chair height; fixed joint (rigid connection); coupled versus uncoupled screw motion (whether turning forces sliding); folding joints in folding chairs, eyeglasses, scissors and pliers (pivot hinges); rotary knobs and switches (hinge with limits); retractable pen (slider) [uncertain: which pens have sliders versus screws]; globe (rotation on a tilted axis); USB stick with swivel cover (hinge) [uncertain]; suitcase telescoping handle (slider) [uncertain]; limited-range joints (motion limits, e.g. 0 to 90 degrees)
coverage.making_methods: Not aimed at making. It is for computer vision, robotics simulation and robot learning (e.g. training robots to open drawers and doors). Its objects are household products whose joints are made by injection moulding, sheet metal and furniture hardware, but the dataset does not describe how they are made
coverage.item_count: 2,346 objects (paper), 46 categories, 14,068 movable parts; the Hugging Face repository lists 2,347 object zip files. Largest categories: storage furniture/cabinet (345 objects, 1,174 parts), table (101), faucet (84), chair (80); keyboards alone have 3,593 movable parts (keys)
coverage.special_behaviours_covered: torque-limiting: no; self-locking: no; hand-release only: no; one-way/ratchet: no; indexing/detent: no (motion limits only; no clicks or detents); over-centre: no; compliant: no (all parts are rigid links; the simulator adds friction and damping values); print-in-place: no; gear trains/gearboxes: no; powered connectors: no; adhesive types: no. The only in-scope-adjacent content is the screw joint (threaded caps) and joint motion limits
coverage.entry_structure: Per object: a URDF file (links and joints with type, axis, origin and limits), textured OBJ meshes, a semantics file listing each moving part with its joint type and label, a mobility JSON file with the motion annotations, PartNet part hierarchy files, bounding box and point samples (file list from a third-party validator page) [uncertain], and preview renders. No descriptions, design rules or how-to
coverage.audience_level: research (computer vision, robotics and robot learning)

usefulness.beginner_friendliness: low. Access needs an approved research request, the data are URDF and mesh files meant for a simulator, and there are no plain-English explanations. The object categories (kettle, stapler, laptop) are familiar, and the three motion names (hinge, slider, screw) are plain words, which helps
usefulness.has_images: yes. Textured 3D models of every object (realistic household items), renders in the paper, and on the original site thumbnail previews [uncertain]. Good visual quality, but not diagrams of the joint mechanism itself
usefulness.has_animations: yes, indirectly. Every object can be animated interactively in the SAPIEN simulator viewer (open drawers, turn caps), and the original website had an interactive 3D preview with movable parts [uncertain: could not be opened]. The paper shows robot manipulation tasks (faucet turning, chair folding) with a supplementary video. No ready-made GIFs
usefulness.gaps: Only three motion types, with no information on HOW a joint is built (what kind of hinge, how a drawer runner or snap works), no holding or locking behaviours (latches, detents, catches, ratchets), no fasteners, gears, springs, powered connectors or adhesives, no design rules, and non-commercial, approval-only access. Everyday products only, so no maker-specific joints such as print-in-place or compliant hinges
usefulness.good_for_entry_links: low. Objects are numbered folders inside zip files on a gated Hugging Face repository, so a beginner cannot open a single object page. The old SAPIEN site may have had per-object preview pages [uncertain: not opened]. The only stable public pages are the dataset card https://huggingface.co/datasets/sapien-sim/PartNetMobility and the paper https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.08515
usefulness.reusable_data: structured but restricted. The dataset is downloadable per object (zip with URDF and JSON annotations) and a metadata.json file exists on Hugging Face (gated, not opened), so joint-type counts per category could be computed by script. Licence: non-commercial research and education only, and ShapeNet terms also apply, so the models and derived images cannot be republished on a public site. The category list and the three motion names are generic and can be reused freely as vocabulary
usefulness.maintained: Yes. The simulator repository is maintained (version 3.x, copyright line updated to 2025 with Hillbot Inc.), its documentation site is live, and the dataset was moved to Hugging Face in July 2026 (last update 30 July 2026; about 810 downloads and 16 likes at the time of checking). The old sapien.ucsd.edu site was unreachable from here; a Wayback Machine snapshot of its browse page from 29 December 2025 exists (listed by the Wayback availability API, not opened) [uncertain]
usefulness.ideas_to_borrow: (1) Use three or four plain motion words as the first 'how does it move' question in the flow chart: turns (hinge), slides (slider), turns and slides together (screw), does not move (fixed). (2) Give each moving joint a motion range (e.g. 'opens 0 to 110 degrees', 'slides 30 mm'), as PartNet-Mobility does with motion limits. (3) Illustrate each joint type with familiar household examples (door hinge, drawer, bottle cap, swivel chair), which beginners recognise immediately. (4) The annotation tool's question-and-answer approach ('Does this part move relative to that one? Does it turn or slide? Does the slide also turn?') is itself a good model for a beginner decision tree. (5) Record whether two motions are coupled (screw: turning forces sliding)
usefulness.design_rules_given: No. Only motion limits (angles, lengths) and simulator physics values (friction, damping, density set to plausible ranges); no clearances, fits, strength or torque figures
usefulness.generator_or_parametric: No geometry generator. The simulator can build articulated objects in code (articulation builder with revolute, prismatic and fixed joints) and load URDFs, but it does not generate connection geometry for making
usefulness.file_formats: URDF (with joints and limits), OBJ textured meshes, JSON annotation files (mobility and PartNet hierarchy), text semantics file, PNG renders [uncertain: exact image files], zip archives per object; the simulator is a Python package (PyPI) with an Apache-2.0 C++/Python code base
usefulness.terminology_value: low to medium. Useful for the plain synonyms used in robotics: hinge = revolute joint, slider = prismatic joint, screw = helical joint, and for everyday examples of each. It has no names for specific connection or mechanism types
usefulness.decision_support: None for makers. There is no selector or comparison. The mobility annotation tool (not public) used a question-and-answer flow to identify fixed, hinged and sliding parts, which is a useful pattern but not a feature of the dataset
usefulness.derived_from_or_overlaps: Built on PartNet (fine-grained part hierarchies) and ShapeNet, whose models come from Trimble 3D Warehouse. Compared in the paper with Shape2Motion (2,440 models, 6,762 motion parts), RPM-Net (949 models) and Hu et al. It is cited as the part-mobility dataset in the JoinABLe and Assemble Them All papers, which contrast it with real CAD assemblies (Fusion 360 Gallery, AutoMate). Its simulator is used by the ManiSkill robot-learning benchmark. Several community mirrors and derivatives exist on Hugging Face (e.g. a QueST-PartNetMobility-SAPIEN dataset and 'partnet-mobility-updated'), seen in search results only [uncertain]
